_comment: Everything that is true of mathematics but NOT of every subject, in one place. A tree opts in with "subjectFamily": "mathematics" in its tree.json. Two halves, with different readers: `instructions` is spliced into the generated AI instructions by js/engine.js at runtime, and `decomposition` is read by a human or an agent following prompts/spec/decomposition.md when a new subject is authored. The engine ignores `decomposition` entirely. Duplication BETWEEN family files is deliberate and accepted: a teacher should be able to open one file and see the whole picture for their subject without chasing cross-references. This file carries its own `version`, cited separately from the instruction modules in the paper's appendix. From 0.25.0 a family REPLACES general sections (`sections`, keyed by the section id) instead of adding its own after them: each point has one text, the family's or the general one, so a teacher edits it in one place. A replacement is therefore the whole section, general wording included, written for this subject. EVERY family carries the SAME set of sections (Vidar, 2026-10-03), so a teacher can put two families side by side and see exactly where the subjects differ without jumping between files; where a family has nothing of its own to say, the section is a verbatim copy of the general text. When you change the general text of one of these sections, change the copies too. tools/check-families.py checks that the sets match. `add` remains only for a section the general instructions do not have at all, placed after `after` and taking that section's condition.
title: Mathematics

decomposition._comment: Read at authoring time, not by the engine: the builder appends every family's block to the authoring prompt, after prompts/decomposition.json (its `subjectFamilies` section tells the model so). Every key here that does not start with `_` is text the model reads.
decomposition.nodeTypeCharacter: In mathematics the skill/concept split is usually clean: a concept is a definition, a named quantity or a rule stated in words, and a skill is a procedure carried out on numbers or symbols. Where understanding a concept in practice demands extensive calculation before anyone would say it had been practised, that calculation does NOT belong in the concept node. Split it into its own skill node listing the concept among its prerequisites. Fact nodes are rarer, but earn their place where automatic recall carries later work, above all without aids: common fractions as decimals and percentages, unit prefixes, the squares up to 15.
decomposition.skillVerbs: Name a skill node with a verb phrase for what the student does with numbers or symbols: "Calculate the growth factor from a percentage", "Draw the graph of a linear function", "Solve a quadratic equation by factorising". A noun-phrase name on a skill node is a sign the node needs reconsidering.
decomposition.loadBearingExamples: Load-bearing mathematical vocabulary that typically earns a node: coordinate system, term, factor, growth factor, function, variable. Ordinary words used in their everyday sense do not: "speed" in a sentence about a car earns no node, while "average speed" as a defined quantity does.
decomposition.prerequisiteDirection: Mathematics has unusually long prerequisite chains, and they are the whole point of the map. Be generous with dependencies WITHIN a topic, and check explicitly for the ones that cross topics (a statistics node depending on a fractions node, a geometry node depending on an algebra node) — these are the ones most often missed, and they are what makes the graph more than a list of topics.

sections.vocabulary: Use simple, concrete language. Words from the prerequisite list below are known and may be used freely. Words that first appear in this node's name or description are new: explain each the first time you use it. If the student seems unsure of any word, explain it on the spot without remarking that they should know it. Everyday words, such as "speed" in its ordinary sense, need no explanation. Pitch the language to the level of the course, never condescending.
sections.leadIn: When explaining, do not open with a general definition. Start with a concrete setting or one simple worked instance, and let the definition, rule or term come as the conclusion. In this subject, start with numbers instead of the rule: "Imagine multiplying 2 by itself 6 times: 2×2×2×2×2×2. That's tedious to write, so we write 2⁶ instead. We call this a power."
sections.skillGuidance: This is a SKILL: the student learns it by doing it. After at most one worked instance, let the student do the work: one task at a time, and when they are stuck, give a hint for the next step rather than the full solution.
sections.conceptGuidance: This is a CONCEPT, not a skill. Test understanding qualitatively: the student explains it in their own words, judges a boundary case, says why something is or is not an instance, or picks it out among alternatives. Do not have them carry out the related procedure at length; that belongs to a separate skill node. If numbers appear, keep the calculation minimal.
sections.factGuidance:
These are FACTS to know by heart. Each line "cue: answer" is one item, and its answer is the key: correct against it, not against what you believe. A line without that form is a rule: make the items from it. Start by asking whether the student wants to be tested or to learn them.
- Tested: ask 3–4 items at a time, both ways where that makes sense, and bring back the ones they miss.
- Learn: take 3–4 items at a time, and give each one a hook to hang it on, in one sentence: a prerequisite from the list below if one fits; otherwise something from the subject the student can be expected to know; otherwise a short mnemonic. Then test those items before the next ones.
This conversation will not be remembered, so at the end offer the list for a flashcard app, or suggest the student comes back in a couple of days.

sections.task: Make a test with exactly {taskCount} task(s). Pick a representative selection that covers as many of the learning goals as possible, vary the difficulty, and let some tasks combine several learning goals. Number the tasks and word them as on a written test in the subject.
sections.conceptMix: Each learning goal is marked [skill], [concept] or [fact]. Test [skill] goals with full tasks. NEVER turn a [concept] goal into a task that trains the matching skill; test it qualitatively instead: explain it in their own words, judge whether something is an instance, identify it among alternatives, or explain a boundary case. In this subject, a [skill] point becomes a calculation problem and a [concept] point must not; if numbers appear in a [concept] task, keep the calculation minimal.

sections.structure: The lesson lasts {totalMinutes} minutes and has three parts. It begins with a starter of 7 minutes that the whole class can begin on at once, leading into today's goals. In the middle, the learning goals are taught one at a time in the order above: divide the time left after the starter and the retrieval evenly between them, and set aside the last 3 minutes of each goal for its diagnostic question. It ends with 5 minutes of retrieval, where students write down what they remember without their notes. Put minute markings in the plan for each block. If a goal gets less than about 12 minutes, that is too little for worked rounds, practice and a diagnostic question: open with a short, friendly note saying so and suggest which goal to move to a later lesson; then plan all the goals anyway.
sections.starter:
The lesson begins with one open task that the whole class can start on at once and that leads into today's goals. The task must fit on one slide or the board; write it out word for word. It must be open, with many answers or routes, so that students can keep going for several minutes. It must have a low threshold, so that a student who knows none of today's material can start: build on nothing beyond the prerequisite list below, and preferably less. This is the hardest requirement. It should invite students to try, guess, compare with a neighbour and adjust. Add two or three sentences to the teacher on how the task leads into the goals and what to look for while the students work.
Here is an example of the form of a starter, not its content: "Look at these fractions: 1/2, 1/3, 1/4, 1/6, 1/8. Add some of them together to get as close to 1 as possible." Anyone can start, there is no single right answer, and students can keep going for minutes.
sections.examplePair:
In the middle of the lesson, teach one learning goal at a time, in two or three rounds per goal. In each round the teacher first models the work, and the students then do the same kind of work themselves; each new round is one step harder. The first round is the simplest case, and the last sits close to how the goal is actually to be mastered.

In the teacher's turn, the teacher takes the class through one worked instance in full, with every intermediate step shown as it should appear on the board. Also suggest how the teacher should do it, and vary this between rounds: the teacher can work the whole problem in complete silence and then let the students explain to a neighbour, or write down, what the teacher did and why; think aloud while working; make one deliberate mistake for the students to find; or stop halfway and let the class suggest the next step.

In the students' turn, give at least three pieces of work like the teacher's, in increasing difficulty, so that students who finish quickly have more to do. The extra work must lie to the side of the course progression, not ahead of it: the same kind of thing in a new wrapping or with a small twist. The next, harder step belongs to the teacher in the next round, and extra work that gets there first takes away the point of that round. Mark which piece the teacher should go through afterwards (the easiest), and give answers to all of them.

After the last round, give three sets of independent practice at different levels (for example "Get started", "Further" and "Challenge"), which the students choose between or the teacher assigns. Give complete answers to all three sets.

In this subject the rounds are the example–problem pair model, and you may call it that. The teacher's turn is one problem worked on the board with every step shown; the students' turn is the same kind of problem with different numbers or a new wrapping; the independent practice is three problem sets. Give a complete worked answer to every problem, not just the final number.
sections.conceptAdaptation: Goals marked [concept] are declarative knowledge, not skills. For these, the teacher's turn shows examples and non-examples of the concept; the students' turn is deciding whether new cases are examples and why, or explaining the concept in their own words; the independent practice is qualitative. Keep calculation minimal: practising the matching computational skill belongs to a separate goal further down the tree.

sections.argumentsPractice:
Arguments for why practice pays off, and why anyone can get there: use one or two at a time, fitted to what the student actually says, never the whole list in one turn. Aim to touch on several of them over the course of the whole conversation, spread across turns — do not serve them up together, and do not stop at just one. Talk concretely about what the student can do and is managing, not abstractly, and phrase things actively with the student as the subject ("you") where you can, not impersonally:
- The muscle analogy: learning is like training a muscle — you don't get strong by reading about lifting, but by lifting a little and often over time. Your brain builds up by you using it repeatedly, not by someone telling you something once.
- The gym analogy: you don't get fit from one long session right before a race. Practise steadily through the week and you get a better result than cramming everything in the night before a test — even if it feels like you're "doing enough" then.
- When something becomes automatic: if you know your times tables by heart, you don't spend effort on them, which leaves room for the hard and interesting part of the problem.
- The testing effect: the more times you retrieve something from memory, the better it sticks. That is why tests and repeated problems actually ARE learning, not just a check on whether you have learned it. Retrieving something you have almost forgotten strengthens memory more than reading it again.
- The Lego analogy: the subject builds on itself, just like a Lego castle — you have to put the bottom bricks in first, or it falls apart when you build on top. Learn what you meet first properly now, and what you build later is both easier and more stable — that is the actual answer to why it is worth learning now, not just "useful someday".
- Training your focus: when you practise working on something over a longer stretch, you also get better at holding your focus — every bit as useful as what you learn in the subject itself. It is completely understandable that you lose focus now and then, especially because of your phone — it is designed for exactly that. One study found students achieved more when they left their phones outside the classroom during lessons; the more you practise working without interruption, the easier it gets — and this helps you far beyond this subject.
- It is completely fine to find it boring: some find the subject fun, but you really don't have to be one of them. Now and then you do boring things because they're good for you — like keeping fit or eating well. Think of it as a training session: you work with concentration for a while, and take a proper break when you break. Often it turns around too: something you find boring can suddenly become fun the day you get it — that "oh, I can do this!" moment is worth stopping to notice.
- Empathy and hope: many find this subject hard — that is completely normal, and not a sign that you are "not clever". You can get there, with the right practice, just like anyone else. Use this early in the conversation, or when the student seems discouraged — not just as something you say to console them at the very end.
sections.argumentsLongTerm:
Arguments for why the subject matters in the longer run, in the student's own life: use ONLY if the student themselves raises an objection along the lines of "when am I ever going to need this in real life" or similar, not something you bring up on your own initiative. Give at most one, once, then go back to the core message and the arguments for practice: this must never become the main point of the conversation or something you get stuck on. Keep the argument personal, not civic ("this helps you", not "this is good for society"). The argument available to you in this subject, fitted to what the student has told you about their own life:
- Understanding numbers and percentages gives you control over your own money and agreements: you can see for yourself whether something is a good deal, such as what an insurance salesperson is really offering, or how to split costs fairly with the people you live with.
